lead: Offshore there is no harbour to run for: read the chart yourself, weigh each forecast, decide early.

sections.title: Which way the wind turns
refs: Pressure systems — wind round a high
Pressure systems — Buys Ballot in the south
Pressure systems — routing round a high

Pressure systems — the col
Pressure systems — Azores high and the heat low

blocks.p: Northern hemisphere: the wind turns **clockwise round a high**, slightly outwards, anticlockwise round a low, slightly inwards; in the south both reverse. **Buys Ballot**: back to the wind, the low is on your left in the north, your right in the south.

A high's centre is nearly calm: route round its fair-wind side. A **blocking high** sits for days and steers the lows round it. A **col**, the saddle between two highs and two lows, gives light, shifting airs, fog or thunder. In summer the Azores high and Iberia's **heat low** drive a northerly down Portugal.

blocks.p: The **jet stream** steers the lows: under a strong, straight jet they race through in series; a **cut-off** low wanders unpredictably. Face the way a low travels (northern hemisphere): the wind **veers** on the right of its track, **backs** on the left.
On the right its motion adds to its wind. Under the centre the wind dies at the lowest pressure, then returns hard from the opposite side.

blocks.p: Triangles mark a cold front, semicircles a warm one; both on one side an **occlusion**, on opposite sides a **stationary front**. An occlusion brings one rain band and one veer, no warm sector.

A **secondary low** forms at the **triple point**, where the fronts meet, or as a wave on a trailing cold front: the wind backs again, rain returns, the glass falls. Its strongest wind lies away from the parent.

blocks.p: After the cold front's veer the old sea crosses the new; time the front by closing speed.

blocks.p: Measure the spacing in miles on the **latitude scale** and enter the **geostrophic scale**, drawn for one interval and latitude: the same spacing gives less wind further north. Round a low the real (**gradient**) wind is less than the scale shows, round a high more; at the sea about 0.8 of that, backed 15°. A prognosis is valid at data time plus step.

fig.title: Wind from the isobars
lines: Tight curve round a low: −15 % → 34 kn

blocks.p: Forecast and Beaufort wind is the 10 m mean; a masthead sensor reads more. Without one, read the sea.

blocks.p: Read your own area, your route's and those to windward. The synopsis says where a low will be and how deep; 'losing its identity' means fading. An **ensemble** runs the model many times: the share of members showing a gale is its chance; a wide spread means low confidence.

lines: 6–9 hPa in 3 h: a gale likely

blocks.p: Believe a gale the bulletin and ensemble show but your GRIB lacks. A coarse grid misses mountain gaps; a measured satellite wind beats the model; laden, divide a router's time by 0.8. Your own log outranks any forecast: allow for the **barometer's** daily swing in the tropics and your own run across the isobars; a slow fall means a long blow.

blocks.p: **Significant height** (Hs) is the mean of the highest third; the biggest wave is nearly twice it. The sea is limited by the smaller of **fetch** and duration. **Swell** runs on from its storm, whatever the local wind. Steepness, not height, breaks crests: a short wind sea beats a higher long swell, worst against a current.

blocks.p: Offshore, **sea room** is safety: drift, hove-to or running, times the gale's hours must fit inside the distance to the lee shore. A port of refuge counts only if you reach it with hours in hand and its entrance is safe in the gale. Give a window a margin; after a gale let the sea go down. A motor yacht's limit is the head sea, not the wind.

blocks.p: Sea fog is **advection fog**: moist air cooled below its dew point by colder water, as over upwelling. It lasts until a cold front brings dry air: pick the wide, buoyed entrance. **Sea smoke** is steam where very cold air crosses warmer water.

fig.note: High island in the NE trade wind

blocks.p: Land on your right looking downwind (northern hemisphere): the wind converges along the coast and freshens; land on your left, it diverges and eases. Swell bends round a point into the bay behind it and reflects off cliffs: a confused sea. An east wind off the Sahara brings the **calima**, dust haze.

Over a warm sea thunderstorms peak at night; high **CAPE** in a GRIB warns of them. Plot a cell on radar like a ship: you cannot outrun it, so reef and pass astern; leave a waterspout's track at right angles. The **gust front** brings a sharp shift and double the wind. St Elmo's fire warns of a strike: crew off the rig, spare electronics in the oven; afterwards check the compass.
